title: NY Permit Test: Flashing Lights and What You Must Do
description: Red, blue, green, or amber lights in New York: when the law says pull over and stop, when it says slow down and move over, and when a school bus means stop.
intro: New York drivers see flashing lights of many colors: red on fire trucks, blue on a volunteer firefighter's own car, green on a volunteer ambulance member's car, amber on snow plows and tow trucks, and red again on a school bus. Each one asks something different of you. Some mean pull over to the right and stop. Some mean slow down and change lanes. Some are only a warning, and one means stop in place and wait. This page sorts them out using the New York State Driver's Manual and the DMV point system page, both checked on November 7, 2026, and shows how the permit test tends to ask about them.

sections.heading: Two questions that sort out almost every case
sections.body:
When you see flashing lights, ask two things before you do anything.

1. **Is the vehicle moving toward me, or is it stopped?** A moving emergency vehicle that is responding to a call gets the right-of-way. A vehicle that is already stopped on the shoulder or in the road falls under a different rule, the Move Over law.
2. **What kind of vehicle is it?** The manual separates authorized emergency vehicles (fire, ambulance, police and other authorized vehicles) from vehicles that only carry warning lights, such as plows, tow trucks, and volunteers' personal cars. School buses have a rule of their own.

Most wrong answers on this topic come from mixing these up, for example treating a stopped police car like a moving one, or treating a green light like a siren.

sections.heading: Moving with red lights and a siren: pull right and stop
sections.body:
The manual says authorized emergency vehicles responding to emergencies show flashing red, red and blue, or red and white lights and sound a siren or air-horn. It also notes that vehicles responding for a Police Department, Sheriff Department, or the State Troopers are not always required to use a siren or horn, so lights alone can be enough.

When one heads toward you from any direction, the manual's steps are:

1. Safely pull over right away to the **right edge** of the road and stop.
2. If you are in an intersection, drive out of it first, then pull over.
3. Wait until the emergency vehicle passes before you drive on.

This applies even when the vehicle is coming toward you in the opposite lane of a two-way road. And if you hear a siren or air-horn close by but cannot tell where it is, the manual says to pull over to the right edge and stop until you are sure it is not headed toward you.

Why so strict? The manual explains that a driver using lights and siren may legally exceed the speed limit, go through red lights and STOP or YIELD signs, drive the wrong way on a one-way street, and turn where others cannot. You cannot predict its path, so the safe move is to clear the way and hold still.

sections.heading: Stopped on the shoulder: the Move Over law
sections.body:
Now picture a police car, ambulance, tow truck, or plow that is already parked or stopped on the shoulder or another part of the road with its lights on. You do not pull over and stop here. The Move Over law asks for two different things depending on the road.

- **On every road:** reduce your speed and take care to avoid hitting the vehicle.
- **On parkways, interstates, and other controlled-access roads with multiple lanes:** also move out of the lane next to the stopped vehicle, unless traffic or another hazard makes that unsafe.

The manual says the law covers authorized emergency vehicles with emergency lights on, hazard vehicles with one or more amber lights on, and hazard vehicles showing amber lights together with blue lights. It also covers vehicles with blue and green lights. On a parkway or controlled-access highway, it even covers any ordinary motor vehicle that is parked, stopped, or standing on the shoulder or in the road, so a stalled car counts there too.

A quick example: on a two-lane country road you pass a tow truck with amber lights on the shoulder. There is no second lane to move into, so the rule for you is to slow down and give it care. On a three-lane interstate, the same tow truck means slow down and also leave the right lane if you can do it safely. A violation is punished as a moving violation.

sections.heading: Blue, green, or amber lights on the move: a courtesy yield
sections.body:
This is the point many test takers miss. According to the manual:

- **Blue lights** may be shown on personal vehicles of volunteer firefighters answering alarms.
- **Green lights** may be shown on personal vehicles of volunteer ambulance or rescue squad members.
- **Amber lights** are on hazard vehicles such as snow plows and tow trucks. Tow and push vehicles may combine amber lights with blue lights that face to the rear. Flashing amber is also used on rural mail delivery vehicles and on school buses to warn traffic.

None of these are authorized emergency vehicles, and their drivers must obey all traffic laws. You are **not required** to yield the right-of-way to them while they are moving, but the manual says you should yield as a courtesy when you can do it safely.

The two rules overlap only when the vehicle stops. A volunteer's car with a blue light that is driving behind you does not have to be given the road. The same car stopped on the shoulder with its light on is covered by the Move Over law described above.

sections.heading: School bus lights: stop where you are, from both directions
sections.body:
A school bus uses lights in two steps. Before it stops to load or let off children, the driver usually flashes **yellow** lights near the roof on the front and back. That means slow down and get ready to stop. When the stopped bus flashes **red**, traffic from either direction must stop before reaching it.

Key details from the manual:

- Stop at least **20 feet** from the bus. Unlike an emergency vehicle, you do not pull to the right edge. You stop and wait.
- The rule applies on all roads in the state, in front of schools, in school parking lots, and even when the bus is on the **opposite side of a divided highway**.
- Do not move until the bus starts moving again or the bus driver or a traffic officer signals you to go. Then drive slowly and look for children along the road.
- Vehicles that carry people with disabilities can be equipped as school buses, and you must stop for them the same way.

The penalties show how seriously the state treats this. Passing a stopped school bus carries **8 points** on the DMV point system. The manual lists fines from at least $250 for a first violation up to $1,000 for three violations in three years, and three convictions in three years bring a license revocation of at least six months. Separately, stop-arm cameras on buses can lead to penalties for the vehicle's owner: $250 for a first violation, $275 for a second within 18 months, and $300 for a third or more within 18 months.

sections.heading: Where the permit test sets its traps
sections.body:
The New York permit test has 20 multiple choice questions, and you need at least 14 correct, including at least 2 of the 4 road sign questions. Lights questions show up as short driving situations. In this site's New York practice set, they sit mostly in the Intersections and Sharing the Road chapters, and the wrong answers follow a pattern you can learn:

- **Stopping in place for a moving fire truck or ambulance.** The answer is the right edge of the road, not your lane and not the left side.
- **Stopping in the middle of an intersection.** Drive through first, then pull right.
- **Staying in your lane at the same speed past a stopped police car.** The answer is slow down and move over when it is safe.
- **Driving on because the school bus is across a divider.** The stop rule still applies on a divided highway.
- **Restarting when the children seem clear or the door closes.** You wait for the bus to move or for the driver or an officer to wave you on.

If an answer choice treats a blue or green light like a siren, read it twice. Moving vehicles with only those lights get a courtesy yield, not a required one.

sections.heading: Your five-minute check before the test
sections.body:
Cover the answers and say out loud what you would do in each case:

1. A fire truck with red lights and siren comes up behind you on a city street.
2. You hear a siren but cannot see where it is coming from.
3. A state police car is stopped on the shoulder of a three-lane interstate.
4. A snow plow with amber lights is parked on the shoulder of a two-lane road.
5. A car with a green light comes up behind you.
6. A school bus across a divided highway stops with red lights flashing.

Answers in short: pull right and stop; pull right and stop until sure; slow down and move out of the next lane if safe; slow down; you may yield as a courtesy if safe; stop and wait. If any of these took you more than a few seconds, run the Intersections and Sharing the Road practice sets on this site once more before your DMV visit.

faq.question: Does the Move Over law apply to a tow truck with amber lights?
faq.answer: Yes. The manual lists hazard vehicles with amber lights on, such as tow trucks and snow plows, among the vehicles covered when they are parked, stopped, or standing on the shoulder or in the road. On any road you must slow down; on a multi-lane controlled-access road you also move out of the next lane if it is safe.

faq.question: What if traffic will not let me change lanes for a stopped police car?
faq.answer: The law asks you to move from the next lane unless traffic or another hazard prevents doing it safely. Slowing down still applies on every road, so if you cannot move over, reduce your speed and pass with care.

faq.question: Can points from passing a school bus lead to a suspension?
faq.answer: Passing a stopped school bus adds 8 points. The DMV says a driver who reaches 11 points within 24 months may have their license suspended, so this one ticket covers most of that limit. Points count by the date of the violation, not the date of conviction.
